summary: This informational document discusses architectural considerations for smart object networking in the Internet of Things, where many embedded devices use Internet protocols and are not operated directly by humans.

plainLanguage.summary: Lots of small gadgets are being put on the internet. This note talks about how to design that so it works well and what to keep in mind.

questions: how to design internet of things systems
subtitle: How to design Internet-connected embedded devices that actually work

tldr.problem: Engineers designing smart objects (embedded devices that connect to the Internet) face complex decisions about which protocols to use, how devices should communicate, and how to ensure they work reliably in a real, deployed Internet infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: The document offers guidance grounded in four design principles: use proven communication patterns from existing deployments; reuse standardized Internet protocols rather than inventing new ones; account for how the actual Internet (with middleboxes, NATs, and other constraints) works; and design systems that can adapt over time.
tldr.outcome: By following these principles, smart object developers can lower design costs, reduce security risks, achieve better interoperability, and create systems that remain relevant as the Internet evolves.

today: RFC 7452 is an Informational document from the Internet Architecture Board providing guidance for IoT and smart object design. It has not been obsoleted. The principles remain relevant for anyone building Internet-connected embedded devices, though newer specific protocols (like MQTT, CoAP, and LoRaWAN) have emerged since publication.

sections.title: The Challenge of Connected Embedded Devices
sections.content:
Smart objects are embedded devices with limited energy, memory, bandwidth, and processing power that connect to the Internet. They range from simple sensors and switches to complex systems like industrial controls and wearables. The term Internet of Things (IoT) describes the trend of putting Internet protocols on ever-smaller devices.

Designing Internet-connected smart objects requires expertise in hardware, software, embedded systems, and Internet protocols—a difficult combination. To simplify development and reduce costs, engineers should reuse proven solutions rather than designing from scratch. This document provides high-level guidance based on four key principles: utilize existing communication patterns, reuse Internet protocols, account for the deployed Internet's realities, and design systems for change.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny devices are hard to design, so it is smarter to copy what already works than to invent something new.

sections.title: Common Communication Patterns
sections.content:
Existing smart object deployments follow four recurring communication patterns, each with different interoperability and design implications:

Device-to-device: Two devices from different manufacturers communicate directly. Example: a light switch controlling a light bulb. This requires vendors to agree on a shared protocol stack, from the physical radio layer through the application layer. It demands the most standardization effort but enables strong interoperability.

Device-to-cloud: Devices send sensor data to a cloud service provider (example.com). A single vendor often controls both the devices and the cloud, so interoperability is optional. However, if third-party devices need to connect, standard protocols (CoAP, HTTP, DTLS, UDP) are essential. The risk is vendor lock-in if the provider shuts down or changes business models.

Device-to-gateway: Devices use non-standard or low-power radios (like IEEE 802.15.4) and communicate through a gateway (a smartphone or router) to the Internet. The gateway translates between the local protocol and Internet protocols. This is common for wearables and home automation but creates a single point of failure and relies on the gateway software to stay updated.

Back-end data sharing: Cloud providers allow third parties to access data collected from devices via APIs (like OAuth 2.0 and REST). This combats data silos but requires that the application layer be standardized as well.

Developers should select or combine these patterns based on their use case and design accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart devices can talk directly to each other, to the cloud, through a gateway, or let companies share data. Each way has trade-offs in effort, lock-in, and fragility.

sections.title: Reuse Standardized Internet Protocols
sections.content:
Reusing existing, standardized protocols is vastly preferable to designing new ones. New protocols are expensive to design, implement, test, and deploy. They require training staff and, potentially, end users. Most importantly, they incur higher security risk because they lack the public review and battle-testing that established standards have undergone.

Internet protocols are designed to be flexible and can be tailored to specific constrained environments. The IETF has developed or standardized many protocols suitable for smart objects: CoAP (a lightweight HTTP alternative), DTLS (datagram security), 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over low-power radios), and many others.

However, some vendors develop proprietary or domain-specific protocols, creating silos. The Internet Protocol Suite is extensive and offers tools like the Web, RESTful APIs, and federated authentication that many developers already know. Using these tools lowers training costs and broadens the developer pool available to build and maintain systems.

The Internet's success comes from using general-purpose, incrementally deployable protocols. Even when constraints are tight, it rarely makes sense to prevent devices from communicating with applications beyond those originally envisioned. Design systems so that devices can interact with multiple applications and providers, not just one.
sections.plainLanguage: Use protocols everyone already knows and has tested extensively. New protocols cost more, break more easily, and need more training. Proven standards are better.

sections.title: Account for How the Internet Actually Works
sections.content:
Protocol designers often assume an idealized network, but the real Internet includes middleboxes (firewalls, NATs, proxies) that interfere with traffic in unexpected ways.

Research studies cited in the document illustrate real-world constraints: approximately half of Internet paths drop packets with IP options, making IP option-based extensions unreliable. Home gateways commonly drop or modify UDP, TCP, DCCP, and SCTP packets, and have highly variable timeout behaviors. NAT traversal for DCCP and SCTP is extremely poor. TCP extension mechanisms are interfered with by middleboxes on at least 25% of paths.

These constraints challenge protocol designers trying to add new features. Even well-intentioned extensions may fail in many deployment scenarios. Smart object protocols must be designed with these realities in mind: use widely deployed transport protocols (UDP, TCP), avoid complex options, and ensure that extensions degrade gracefully if middleboxes modify or drop them.

The end-to-end principle—that intelligence should reside in end nodes rather than in the network—remains valuable, but may be challenged by the sheer scale of smart object deployments. Networks sometimes must implement intermediaries. However, networks that remain transparent to data and do not filter or transform content enable the deployment of new services without core network changes, a key contributor to the Internet's success.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet has obstacles (like firewalls and old equipment) that block some messages. Smart devices must work around these obstacles, not assume a perfect network.

sections.title: Design Systems That Evolve Over Time
sections.content:
Internet protocols and preferred technologies evolve constantly. Long-lived smart object deployments must adapt to changing conditions, new threats, and improved capabilities. Design systems for change by using modularity, choice, and software updates.

Modularity breaks complex systems into independent parts so that changes in one area do not disrupt others. Open interfaces enable different parties to make choices that reflect their conflicting interests and preferences.

Software updates are essential. Most operating systems and applications receive regular updates; smart objects should too. Updates are needed to fix security bugs, improve interoperability, and add new features. However, this requires spare flash memory and RAM for the update mechanism, a trade-off worth making for devices with any lifespan beyond a few months.

Device capabilities improve over time. Microelectronics become cheaper and more capable, even as the desire to embed communications in smaller objects continues. Design systems not just for today's constraints but for tomorrow's improved capabilities. Avoid designs that assume devices will never be upgraded or that lock in decisions made at manufacture time.

The document notes that JavaScript-based web applications demonstrate rapid update mechanisms: code is downloaded from many sources and executed in browsers, providing security review through reputation and sandboxing. Similar dynamic mechanisms can work for smart objects if designed in.
sections.plainLanguage: Things will change: new threats, new features, new devices. Smart systems must allow themselves to be updated without being thrown away.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Security is critical for smart objects because they interact directly with the physical world and operate unattended. Constrained devices have fewer resources for security implementation, making secure design essential. At the same time, design decisions have privacy implications even when not explicitly focused on privacy.

Security aspects: Devices must bootstrap trust securely. They may face physical compromise via timing attacks, power analysis, or glitching; distinguish physically secure from exposed devices in the trust model. When thousands of identical devices are deployed, compromising one can enable attacks on the entire collection; avoid sharing secrets across a product family. Devices may be deployed in unexpected ways; minimize impact of misuse. Many devices operate for 5 to 40 years, so design paths to deploy new security mechanisms during the device's lifetime. Security protocols require good randomness, which is challenging in embedded devices; consider hardware-based generators early. Reusing standardized protocols with proven security review is much safer than developing mechanisms in isolation.

Privacy aspects: Users and affected parties must understand what personal data is collected, stored, and why. Collect only data adequate, relevant, and not excessive for the purpose; use anonymized data wherever possible. Clearly define who can access data and under what conditions. Use standardized security measures and robust cryptographic techniques to prevent unlawful access, alteration, or loss. Privacy considerations extend beyond engineering into legal and policy realms, but engineers must design systems that enable privacy compliance.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny devices are targets for attackers. Design them assuming they could get stolen or misused. Also protect people's personal data: be clear what you collect, why, and who sees it. Don't collect more than needed.
